title: Incident Room
pitch: An agent fills the rollback plan on the page you are viewing. The WebMCP form leaves submission to you: narrow the scope, review the operation, press Submit.
about_excerpt: An agent fills the rollback plan on the page you are viewing. The WebMCP form leaves submission to you: narrow the scope, review the operation, press Submit. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT's Sources panel: the agent called inspect_current_incident twice and show_change_comparison once, all tools this page registered. The agent filled the Recovery Plan and stopped. The operator removed healthy payment from scope, so the plan is marked HUMAN EDITED. RECOVERED only after a real Cloudflare rollback returned the same fixed request to 200. Three permanent-fix paths follow, the human picks. PLAN_STALE: someone deployed while the plan was open, so the server refused and wrote no rollback. The plan is refreshed, not restarted. The problem Checkout starts returning 500 right after a deployment. An agent can inspect the incident and prepare a rollback plan, but a person still has to decide which production services get touched and when that plan becomes a real write. In the workflow I wanted to improve, that decision lived in a chat window. The agent described a plan, the person typed "yes", and production changed before the person had reviewed the operation on screen. The approval was real. The review was not. Incident Room puts that decision on the page. The agent fills one Recovery Plan, the person edits it, and the person presses Submit. What the model cannot do The WebMCP form has no toolautosubmit . The agent can fill the fields, but its tool call stays pending until a person submits the form. The Controller also checks the Worker name, target version, scope, and observedDeploymentId against a server-side allowlist. Those values are not open parameters, so the agent can't widen the operation. The page waits for server verification before showing RECOVERED. Why WebMCP fits The Recovery Plan is page state shared by the agent and the person looking at it. A remote MCP server may read the same incident data, but it does not automatically know what this tab currently contains, what the person just edited, or which deployment ID was visible when the plan was drafted. WebMCP lets both parties work on that object in place. I also checked the human gate directly: three seconds after the agent filled the form, the fields were populated and the tool promise had not settled. What changes for the operator The reviewer reads a form, not a paragraph. It shows the Worker, target version, included and excluded services, and the evidence required for success. In the demo, the agent initially includes checkout and payment. Payment is healthy, so the operator removes it with one click before submitting. That correction is visible on the same screen instead of being buried in a chat log. What people and agents can do together A plan can survive a refusal. If another deployment happens while the form is open, the Controller returns PLAN_STALE and performs zero writes. The agent reads the new page state and refreshes the existing plan instead of starting over. After recovery, the agent can call propose_remediation_options with a diagnosis and one of three paths: fix forward through a reviewed pull request, keep investigating on the rollback, or prepare an emergency hotfix. The person still chooses. How I implemented WebMCP Three imperative tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() inside a React effect. An AbortController removes them when the page goes away. inspect_current_incident reads live health and deployment IDs, then focuses the affected service. show_change_comparison opens a diff only for a change already listed in the incident. propose_remediation_options places a diagnosis and repair options on the recovered page. These tools update page state but do not write to an external system. They carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint , while the real authorization boundary remains in the Controller. The Recovery Plan is the declarative tool. It has toolname and tooldescription , but no toolautosubmit . Its submit handler uses SubmitEvent.respondWith() so the page and the agent receive the same result. What is real The lab uses three dedicated Cloudflare Workers, not mocks. A deployed checkout version returns 500. The Controller calls the Workers Deployments API to roll back, then replays the same cart request. RECOVERED appears only when that request returns 200. Cloudflare supplies the deployment IDs shown as evidence. I ran the full path in ChatGPT's built-in browser on GPT-5.6 Sol. I also ran it in Chrome 152 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , including the stale-plan case where the deployment list contained the competing deployment and no rollback. Boundaries There is no remote MCP server, generic connector, or multi-user platform. The public site shares one lab, so another rehearsal can make an open plan stale. Workers Logs are secondary evidence. The permanent-fix step produces a simulated issue draft and labels it as such. It does not call GitHub or claim that a pull request exists. video_transcript_excerpt: An agent can find the bad deployment and write a correct rollback faster than the person on call. It should not be the one that presses the button. Today that approval is one sentence in a chat window and production changes without anyone reviewing the plan. A remote MCP server reads the same incident data, but it cannot reach the page the human is looking at. Web MCP lets this page hand the agent its own tools, so both sides end up editing one object they can both see. None of this is mocked. Three dedicated Cloudflare workers. The controller checks the worker, the version, the scope, and the observed deployment ID against a server-side allow list before it calls the deployments API. Then it replays one fixed checkout request. 500 to 200 or the page never says recovered. Checkout is returning 500 after a deployment. This page is incident room open in chat GPT's built-in browser. The operator asks for recovery plan. Nothing about this prompt tells the agent how the page works. It finds out by asking the page. Incident room registers its tools with Web MCP, so the browser hands the agent a list of what this tab can do. Here are the calls it actually made. Inspect current incident twice. Show change comparison once. Every one of them is a tool this page registered. The comparison tool returns the regression and one instruction. Fill the visible fields for human review, but do not submit it. The recovery plan is a declarative Web MCP form with no auto submit attribute. The agent fills it in and submission is left to the operator. Its draft would rollback checkout and payment. Payment never broke. The operator removes it and the plan is marked human edited. The operator submits. The page keeps a decision history where the agents reads and the humans edits it side by side. This is a real Cloudflare deployment. The same fixed checkout request comes back 200 and only then does the page say recovered. With the outage over, three permanent fixed paths appear. The agent can refine the recommendation from the evidence it just watched. The person still chooses. The agent also writes the plan up. Rollback target, execution gate, abort conditions. The write-up on the left, the tool calls that produced it on the right, and it's closing line. It did not activate the human submit control.

live_observation.first_impression: A guided Incident Room clearly explains a live recovery sequence from observed 500s through rollback, human approval, verification, and remediation.
live_observation.after_state: The guided flow advanced from its landing state and exposed the recovery workflow controls/evidence for progressing through the incident.
live_observation.notes: The page distinguishes agent preparation from required human submission and shows checkout degraded versus payment healthy.
